The recurring circulation of rumors, leaks and unofficial anticipations about skins, champions, events and reconfigurations of the game environment makes it possible to identify, in the Riot Games ecosystem, an especially relevant zone of private administration of expectation that is not exhausted by the platform's formal communication. The legally <1>p. 784</1> relevant point does not lie in asserting, simplistically, that all unofficial information must be attributed directly to the company, nor in presuming absolute control over any parallel circulation of signs within the community. The problem is a different one. It is a matter of recognizing that, in ecosystems of continuous enjoyment, the consumer's expectation can also be organized in a functionally effective way through informal channels, provided that these channels stabilize in the environment as predictable circuits of anticipation, desire and preparation of economic conduct. In that case, the formal announcement ceases to be the only relevant center for shaping trust.

Hypercuratorial anticipation, already delimited as a mechanism for governing the present and the future of enjoyment, takes on a specific form here. It does not operate only through <1>roadmaps</1>, <2>teasers</2>, <3>trailers</3>, <4>dev blogs</4>, seasons or express announcements. It can also operate through unofficial circuits of curated rumor, in which partial images, technical references, fragmentary leaks, presumed calendars and speculations reputed plausible are organized by <5>leakers</5>, influencers and channels specialized in narratives of a consumable future. The rumor, in this context, does not remain mere noise external to the supply. It comes to perform an ordering function, because it introduces a temporality of pre-enjoyment in which the user ranks expectations, postpones present decisions, reserves resources and reorganizes their economy of desire on the basis of unconfirmed signals that are nonetheless socially stabilized as relevant.

The essential aspect does not lie in the abstract existence of anticipation, but in the economic productivity of its unofficial operationalization. When the content circulates without official confirmation, the platform preserves a margin of plausible deniability and strategic flexibility to reformulate schedules, alter products, recalibrate offers or simply harvest reactions without fully assuming, in communicational terms, what was anticipated. At the same time, the expectation stays in circulation, engagement intensifies and the community remains in a state of interpretive readiness. An asymmetric arrangement is thus produced in which the semiotic and economic dividends of anticipation can be captured without proportional absorption of the legal and communicational burdens of the formal announcement. Ambiguity then ceases to be a mere transparency deficit and comes to function as a potential technique for governing expectation.

This dynamic is especially relevant in Immaterial Objects of Consumption because, in them, the will to consume is not formed only at the classical instant of the express offer. It is built in a prolonged ambience of signs, promises, updates and reconfigurations, in which the user learns to wait, to interpret, to bet and to position themselves in the face of possible futures of enjoyment. In such environments, consumption is preceded by a temporal <1>p. 785</1> economy of expectation. One does not buy only the available object. One also buys on account of the anticipated object, the sensed event, the awaited <2>skin</2>, the imagined update. The future comes to organize the present of consumption. That is why stabilized and functionally exploitable rumors can form part, even if obliquely, of the effective governance of the ecosystem.

Influencers and specialized intermediaries perform a particularly relevant function in this process. They are a mass of agents responsible for converting scattered technical data into an emotionally intelligible narrative, stabilizing leaks as plausible promise, transforming fragmentary material into a horizon of expectation and thereby keeping the community in continuous mobilization around what has not yet been officially made available by the developer. Their role is not merely informative. It is also semiotic and economic. They produce interpretive cohesion around the rumor and, with that, allow ambiguous signs to begin influencing spending plans, purchase priority, willingness to wait and the ranking of interest within the ecosystem. The rumor then ceases to be mere community talk and comes to function as an informal infrastructure for administering desire.

The dogmatic usefulness of the point lies in showing that, in contexts of hypercuratorial anticipation, the consumer's trust can be materially shaped outside the traditional limits of the formally delimited offer. This aggravates semiotic vulnerability, because the user comes to decide on the basis of signs that are at once effective and displaced. Effective, because they guide real economic conduct. Displaced, because they remain formally unassumed, hindering direct attribution of liability and making it harder to reconstruct the link between the administration of expectation and the practical impact on enjoyment. The environment thus produces a sophisticated form of strategic opacity. The sign circulates with enough social force to govern decisions, but with enough legal ambiguity to protect, at least in part, whoever benefits from its effectiveness.

The hypothesis upheld here does not depend on proving the platform's absolute dominion over all informal circulation. That objection, although frequent, misses the target. The legal problem does not lie in demanding full control of the origin of each leak, each channel or each speculation. It lies in recognizing that, once a specific, repeated expectation materially apt to guide consumption decisions has settled in the ecosystem, the platform no longer remains in a neutral position. It can administer that expectation through strategic silence, calculated evasion, categorical denial, later incorporation of the anticipated content or simple functional tolerance of the circulation that keeps the environment in a state of engagement and readiness. What matters, therefore, is not absolute sovereignty over the birth of the sign, but <1>p. 786</1> responsibility for managing the expectation once it has come to form, in a relevant way, part of the consumer's decision-making economy.

From this perspective, it becomes possible to consider a normative consequence proportional to the real limits of the platform's governance. It is not a matter of imposing an impracticable duty to prevent every rumor, every leak or every community speculation. Nor is it a matter of turning the company into a universal certifier of hearsay. What can be demanded, in a key compatible with the IOC regime, is something more delimited and institutionally defensible: a duty of clarification, non-contradiction and justification when ecosystemically relevant rumors, endowed with sufficient social credibility and functionally apt to influence spending plans, purchase priority or the wait for enjoyment, are the object of specific prompting by users or become persistently integrated into the consumption environment. Omission, in this framework, ceases to be a simple neutral communicational choice and may become a relevant informational insufficiency in a context of operative expectation.

This framing makes it possible to distinguish dogmatically different situations. The first is that of silence or an evasive answer in the face of an expectation already stabilized and economically influential. In it, the problem may lie in the strategic refusal to administer information materially relevant to the consumer's planning. The second is that of a specific denial later contradicted by a substantially equivalent practice of the platform itself. In that case, the contradiction between communication and conduct may acquire its own weight for the examination of deceptiveness and of legitimately formed trust. The third is that of the confirmation or positive inducement of an expectation later frustrated without proportional clarification. Here, the question is no longer limited to the absence of delivery, but reaches a reinforced duty of transparency, justification and possible restoration compatible with the consolidated trust. In all these situations, the point is not to punish the mutability proper to continuous digital services, but to prevent their structural flexibility from being converted into communicational immunity.

The theoretical gain of this shift is significant. It shows that, in IOCs, consumer protection cannot remain hostage to the classical model of an offer that is formally delimited, instantly verifiable and externally separable from the community ambience that precedes it. In ecosystems of continuous enjoyment, trust begins to be produced before the express announcement and outside the traditional limits of the isolated advertising piece. What is governed is not only the final purchase, but the temporality of waiting, the reserve of desire, the willingness to postpone, the affective economy of the future. When the platform exploits, tolerates or administers gray zones of socially curated expectation, liability tends to <1>p. 787</1> fall less on the isolated origin of each sign and more on the way private governance responds to its practical effectiveness in organizing the consumer's conduct.

Thus, in ecosystems of continuous enjoyment, strategic opacity is not only a passive transparency deficit. It may be an active technique for the economic exploitation of ambiguity. Therefore, the control of the IOC must also reach the informalized zones of administration of expectation, whenever they cease to be spontaneous community noise and come to form, functionally, part of the governance of desire, waiting and consumption planning. The rumor, when it stabilizes as a social infrastructure of pre-enjoyment, is no longer outside the legal problem. It becomes one of its subtlest and most dogmatically demanding forms.

The application of the regime of the Immaterial Object of Consumption to environments of trust administration starts from a structural fact that usually escapes the more traditional legal reading. In platform-governed ecosystems, the conflict does not begin when the user decides to litigate, complain or formalize disagreement. In many cases, it is governed before that. The architecture of the environment, the interface language, the response protocols, the communicational tone, the signs of closeness and the ordinary management of expectation <1>p. 781</1> can operate as mechanisms for the prior absorption of critical resistance, the accommodation of loss and the practical neutralization of contestation. The utility supplied, in these cases, is not limited to the main object of consumption. It also includes a functionally administered regime of trust, by which the environment organizes the way the user interprets friction, metabolizes frustration and decides whether or not the experience suffered deserves institutional translation.

This point is important because it prevents the analysis of the supply from remaining confined to the written contract, to the formally provided information or to the isolated clause governing a given aspect of the relationship. On platforms, trust is not a spontaneous by-product of good performance of the service. Frequently, it is produced, calibrated and maintained by design. The cordial interface, the assistive tone, the diffuse promise of care, merely performative transparency, the appearance of communicational horizontality and the calculated personalization of language materially make up the environment of enjoyment. They do not function merely as brand ornament. They function as a technique for governing perception, organizing the threshold from which loss will be perceived as acceptable, abuse will be read as a minor failure and contestation will be perceived as unnecessary, premature or disproportionate.

That is why, in this family, trust administration must be treated as a functional dimension of the supply itself. The user does not consume only access, utility, content or performance. They consume an environment that presents itself as intelligible, assistive, responsive and, to some extent, worthy of practical credit. This trust need not take the solemn form of an express guarantee to produce relevant legal effects. It is enough that it act in a stable way on the ordinary interpretation of the experience and on the user's willingness to endure friction, accept vague justifications, normalize losses and remain in the cycle of use even when enjoyment has already been functionally degraded. The platform, in this context, does not administer only initial adherence. It administers tolerance of harm and the user's energy to react.

This administration becomes especially sensitive in environments of continuous consumption, in which the relationship is not exhausted in a single act of acquisition and in which small frustrations can be absorbed, reinterpreted and reintegrated into the ordinary flow of the experience. Loss ceases to appear as an exceptional event and comes to be metabolized as part of the normal functioning of the system. The same happens with friction. Instead of promptly triggering a reading of inadequacy or abusiveness, it can be reconfigured by the platform as a technical adjustment, a temporary limitation, an understandable inconvenience, a security measure, a necessary update or a simple stage of use. The language of the environment, in this process, does not <1>p. 782</1> merely describe the frustration. It administers it. And, by administering it, it redefines the very time at which the conflict emerges institutionally.

In this key, trust ceases to be a psychologically vague element and becomes a precise dogmatic problem. What matters is not whether the user “felt” more or less welcomed, but whether the platform structured signs, routines and protocols capable of shifting the reading of loss, reducing the critical force of the experience and weakening the probability of intelligible contestation. Persona, operational cordiality, messages of closeness, excessively reassuring simplifications, answers with an explanatory appearance and service circuits designed to absorb disagreement without effective reconstruction of the problem can operate, together, as a technique of demobilization. Trust, thus, is no longer merely subjective credit deposited by the user. It is a private mechanism for organizing the reception of harm.

The central vulnerability of this subtype is, once again, semiotic vulnerability, but now intensified by the management of trust as a form of modulating resistance. The user is not only facing an opaque environment or criteria they do not control. They are facing an ecosystem that produces signals of intelligibility and care sufficient to induce accommodation, even when the materiality of enjoyment has already been compromised. The result is relevant. Contestation can be postponed, demobilized or dissolved before it acquires institutional form. The conflict does not disappear. It is governed in its pre-legal phase, through mechanisms that turn loss into tolerable noise, opacity into normality and asymmetry into absorbable experience.

This point calls for caution so as not to turn all corporate cordiality into unlawfulness. The problem does not lie in the use of accessible language, in polite customer service or in the legitimate attempt to maintain a functionally stable relationship with the user. The problem begins when these elements come to form, structurally, part of a regime of practical neutralization of conflict. The platform may, for example, offer a sense of transparency without delivering real intelligibility, produce an impression of listening without opening effective avenues of contestation, mobilize a human tone without assuming proportional duties of reasoning or justification and distribute signs of care that function less as adequate information and more as semiotic cushioning of criticism. In these cases, trust administration ceases to be a quality of the service and becomes a technology for containing resistance.

The evidence compatible with this subtype requires reconstruction of the discursive and procedural environment in which frustration becomes legible or, on the contrary, is diluted. This includes analysis of the interface language, the customer service flows, the response templates, the <1>p. 783</1> explanation routines, the way the platform frames loss and the stages through which the user is led to accept, wait, relativize or close the disagreement. It also requires attention to recurring blind spots. The first is the tendency to consider the discursive dimension of the supply irrelevant, as if only clauses and formal acts produced legal effects. The second is the tendency to treat trust as a private feeling of the user, and not as a functional arrangement of the environment. The third is the tendency to suppose that the conflict begins only when an external complaint or litigation arises, ignoring that the platform can govern precisely the moment at which loss becomes institutionally perceptible.

The possible dogmatic consequence, in this subtype, is not reduced to a classical informational defect nor exhausted in misleading advertising in the strict sense, although it may engage with both. The problem tends to gravitate around qualified informational insufficiency, abusive practice through opaque administration of expectation and, in denser cases, abusive teleology when the neutralization of contestation proves to be integrated into the ordinary functioning of the ecosystem. The legal response compatible with this framework tends to require more than simple retrospective reparation. It may call for correction of customer service flows, reinforcement of intelligibility, prohibition of functionally misleading discursive routines, procedural duties of reasoning and the design of avenues of contestation that serve not merely to absorb disagreement, but to make it effectively processable and verifiable.

The usefulness of the subtype lies precisely in making visible a form of governance that usually escapes the radar of traditional control. In many environments, the platform does not need to formally prevent conflict in order to reduce it. It is enough to administer the way it is perceived. It is enough to organize tolerance, semiotic pacification and the metabolization of friction within the very cycle of enjoyment. The control of the IOC, therefore, cannot remain tied to formal information or to the written contract. It must reach the way the environment produces meaning, distributes trust and governs the very practical emergence of contestation. It is on this plane that the neutralization of conflict by architecture ceases to look like a mere communicational detail and reveals itself as a material element of the governed supply.

The stabilization of the regime of the Immaterial Object of Consumption makes it possible to advance to a plane of typological application in which the usefulness of the dogmatic construction can be tested in distinct ecosystems, without this implying conceptual dilution, sectoral drift or rhetorical expansion of the concept. The point, here, is not to gather digital examples under a single heading by mere technological affinity, nor to suggest that every contemporary platform reproduces, with identical intensity, the same form of vulnerability, opacity or capture of enjoyment. What is sought is to verify whether the regime constructed retains a recognizable capacity for incidence when projected onto typical models of continuous digital supply whose organization, although varied in appearance, presents relevant functional equivalences as to the governance of the experience, the administration of intelligibility and the asymmetric distribution of the costs of evidence, permanence and contestation.

The application, therefore, does not rest on superficial similarity between sectors, nor on technological identity between services. The criterion of approximation is structural. What matters is to identify families of platform in which diverse arrangements of private governance administer, by their own means, analogous problems of enjoyment, opacity, verifiability and restoration. The unit of examination lies not in the economic branch nor in the marketing label of the service, but in the predominant mechanism by which the user's experience is organized, modulated, reconfigured or made contestable. It is this mechanism, and not the name of the sector, that provides the basis of comparability and allows the incidence of the IOC to operate as a transposable grammar of reading and decision.

This methodological option fulfills an important dogmatic function. It prevents the typology from turning into a catalog of digital markets, an impressionistic survey of cases or a sociological taxonomy of platforms. The legal interest does not lie in describing sectors out of classificatory curiosity, but in recognizing recurring regimes of continuous digital supply in which enjoyment is governed by architecture, by curation, by administered visibility, by functional opacity, by ordinary mutability or by selective <1>p. 756</1> mechanisms of sanction and prioritization. By shifting the focus from the sector to the governance mechanism, the analysis preserves methodological unity and prevents the application from depending on the interpreter's cultural familiarity with the environment examined. What matters is not whether the platform presents itself as a cognitive tool, market infrastructure, productive environment or reputation system, but how it organizes access, modulates expectations, distributes risks and conditions the possibility of institutional reconstruction of the conflict.

To maintain this comparability, the exposition will follow a constant sequence. In each typical model, it starts from the structural governance mechanism that organizes enjoyment and produces the characteristic friction of the environment. Next, that mechanism is traced back to the central vulnerability it activates, as well as to the way in which promises, expectations and losses are manufactured, administered or degraded over the course of the relationship. In the following stage, the adequate evidence and the evidentiary requirements compatible with the specific form of the conflict are set, including the blind spots that usually hinder its institutional translation. Only then is the possible dogmatic consequence indicated, always by recognizable derivation from the operative grid previously consolidated.

With this, the applied typology ceases to be an exemplifying exercise and comes to function as a test of transposability. What one seeks to demonstrate is that the IOC regime maintains internal coherence when confronted with distinct ecosystems, precisely because its incidence does not depend on the appearance of the environment, but on the structure of private power that organizes it. If the construction is dogmatically consistent, it must be able to recognize, in diverse families of platform, equivalent problems of governed enjoyment, institutionally relevant opacity, asymmetry of meaning and evidentiary asymmetry, without losing precision and without turning into a totalizing metaphor. The value of the typology lies precisely there. It verifies whether the grammar is robust enough to operate outside the laboratory in which it was densified, preserving decisional usefulness and argumentative discipline.

This passage also makes it possible to show that the contemporary mutation of supply is not reduced to the digitization of media or the technical mediation of already known interactions. In many of these environments, the platform comes to govern not only the delivery of utilities, but the very conditions under which those utilities can be perceived, compared, contested, restored or socially stabilized as part of the consumer's experience. That is why the transposition of the regime should not be read as a classificatory adventure. It is, rather, a matter of gauging to what extent the logic of governed enjoyment, open auditability, functional equivalence, semiotic vulnerability and abusive <1>p. 757</1> teleology remains apt to organize the institutional reading of conflicts that, although distinct in appearance, partake of the same structural rationality of supply.

What will follow, therefore, is not a sequence of sectors, but a succession of typical models of incidence. Each of them corresponds to a recurring form of governance of enjoyment on contemporary platforms. Each of them makes it possible to observe how the same grid of controllability behaves in the face of specific problems of promise, trust, opacity, mutability, sanction, reputation, intermediation or administration of expectation. And each of them contributes to showing that the Immaterial Object of Consumption is not a closed sectoral category, but a dogmatic instrument apt to translate, in a legally controllable key, the multiplication of private ecosystems that organize the user's experience as a continuous regime of supply.

The typological transposition carried out makes it possible to draw a more dogmatically relevant result than the mere illustrative expansion of the field of incidence of the Immaterial Object of Consumption. What the adherence tests make visible is that the keys of the regime do not remain dependent on the original laboratory in which they were formulated. On the contrary, they prove traceable to structural and functional equivalences between distinct ecosystems, even when those ecosystems diverge sharply in sectoral appearance, in technological language or in the immediate object of circulation. The common point lies not on the surface of the environment, but in the way enjoyment is governed, expectation is administered, intelligibility is modulated and contestation is made more or less practicable by private design.

This result matters because it moves the IOC regime from a merely inventive position to an effectively decidable one. The usefulness of the category lies not in producing new nomenclature to describe the digitization of economic life, but in offering stable criteria to recognize when, why and under what conditions certain forms of continuous supply require common legal treatment. Governed enjoyment, semiotic vulnerability, evidentiary asymmetry and private modulation of the environment thus cease to appear as scattered impressions about specific sectors and come to make up an institutionally reusable vocabulary. Without this effort of typification, structurally analogous conflicts would tend to be absorbed by the system as disconnected incidents, episodic discomforts or one-off contractual disputes, losing precisely the functional unity that makes them legally comparable.

<1>p. 788</1> At the same time, the typological transposition makes it possible to identify something perhaps even more important. In many of these ecosystems, the environment that governs enjoyment is the same one that governs the way frustration will be perceived, the language by which it will be justified, the difficulty of proving it and the channels through which any dissent may be neutralized even before it turns into an institutionalizable conflict. The problem, then, no longer lies only in the content of the loss or in the intensity of the harm individually experienced. It also lies in the private administration of the conditions under which that loss becomes narratable, demonstrable and contestable. This fact explains why certain disputes seem small when observed in isolation, but reveal a much denser structure when reconstructed from the modulation mechanisms that produce them.

By keeping distinguishable, in each family of platform, the mechanism of injurious modulation, the corresponding evidentiary problem and the rationality of restoration required by the regime, both empty abstraction and casuistic dispersion are avoided. Injurious modulation is not to be confused with its proof. The evidentiary difficulty is not to be confused with the injury itself. And adequate restoration cannot be deduced automatically from traditional categories that treat every loss as susceptible of undifferentiated monetization. In ecosystems of continuous enjoyment, these three dimensions need to be seen in connection, but not in collapse. It is this internal distinction that allows the IOC regime to preserve density and usefulness, instead of becoming a formula too broad to guide any concrete response.

What emerges from the analysis of the models is not, therefore, the conclusion that the IOC would serve for almost everything. What emerges is something far more demanding and more useful. It becomes clear what effectively changes when the incidence of the regime is recognized. The way of narrating the conflict changes, because attention shifts from the isolated event to the supply program. The way of proving changes, because the opacity of the environment ceases to be taken as a neutral fact and comes to be treated as part of the legal problem itself. And the way of remedying changes, because the response can no longer automatically be satisfied with pecuniary equivalents whenever the injury reaches continuity, intelligibility, functional position, practical trust or conditions of permanence in enjoyment.

The typological path shows that the controllability of the IOC does not depend on freezing innovation, imposing absolute transparency or turning every platform into a parastatal entity. It depends on something more sober and more defensible. It depends on bringing the private governance of the environment back to verifiable standards of intelligibility, evidence, equivalence and correction. When this does not occur, precariousness ceases to be a mere contingent trait of the <1>p. 789</1> digital and comes to function as the ordinary mode of organizing the consumer's experience. It is precisely against this naturalization of precariousness that the regime asserts itself.<2> </2>

The stabilization of the legal regime of the Immaterial Object of Consumption allows a further movement. It is no longer a matter of justifying its normative existence, but of testing its capacity for incidence in ecosystems other than the one in which its formulation was originally densified. The legally relevant point does not lie in asserting that every continuous digital provision is subject to the same framing, nor in expanding the concept on the mere ground that economic life has been digitized. What matters is to verify in which functional contexts certain recurring arrangements of private governance, operative opacity and ordinary mutability reorganize, in a structurally similar way, the conditions of access, permanence, intelligibility and contestation of enjoyment, producing an environment apt to receive the same regime of control.

The typology mobilized here is neither sectoral nor merely technological. Its axis is functional and structural, in an analytical key and without claim to exhaustiveness. It does not serve, for example, to dwell on classical strict functional IOCs<1><2>815</2></1>, such as digital tools for editing images, audio or video, whose qualification tends to be more evident when the contracted utility is organized as an enjoyment bundle sustained over time, dependent on account, access, updatable functionalities, libraries, files and continuous modulation by the platform. It seeks, rather, to recognize typical models of incidence from the recurrence of mechanisms that, although they appear in diverse markets, perform legally comparable functions in the organization of the consumption experience.

The test, therefore, is not satisfied with superficial affinities. It requires showing that categories such as semiotic vulnerability, open auditability, functional value equivalence and abusive teleology remain operable when moved to other platform environments, retaining the aptitude to guide the reading of the facts, the organization of evidence and the determination of legal consequences. Without this, the concept would degrade into a classificatory <1>p. 714</1> metaphor. The operation that follows is, thus, expansive without being inflationary. The underlying question is not how many environments can be nominally drawn into the orbit of the IOC, but in which contexts the combination of continuous supply, private governance and structural mutability produces a specific form of legally protectable enjoyment, whose discipline can no longer be adequately resolved by the traditional categories of the one-off circulation of goods and services.

The analysis then turns to typical models of continuous digital supply and platform governance, with special attention to contemporary ecosystems in which opacity, mutability and private direction of the experience are ordinary conditions of the provision. Its aim is to make visible the recurrence of structural forms of organization of continuous immaterial consumption and to verify to what extent the regime already formulated retains, in these environments, its force of qualification, evidence and remedy.

Here, classical strict functional IOCs means the immaterial objects of consumption whose main utility presents itself in a more directly operational way, such as programs, accounts, libraries, files, tools and digital functionalities exploited under continuous provision. Their identification as IOCs stems from the very organization of the supply as an enjoyment bundle sustained over time, subject to access, updating, interoperability, functional preservation and unilateral modulation by the supplier. Thus, the removal or relevant degradation of an essential functionality in editing software, the unjustified restriction of access to an account that concentrates files and libraries, or the substantial alteration of the conditions of use of contracted tools may affect the very object enjoyed, and not merely an accessory convenience of the provision. The reference to such IOCs, at this point, serves only to distinguish them from the less intuitive models examined in the typology, in which the incidence of the IOC depends on recognizing structural functions of governance, intermediation, visibility, reputation, productivity or trust. <1>↩</1>

The journey undertaken in this work began with the finding that there is a type of consumption in which the subject imagines being on his own ground, but moves only within a floor that is granted, revocable and reconfigurable. This was not, from the outset, an ornamental figure, but an institutional description. The access, the permanence and the meaning of what was acquired become dependent on continuous administration that does not present itself as management, but as technical normality. It is precisely this camouflage that makes the conflict hard to see, hard to say and, therefore, hard to protect against.

If Law is the language of the earthly gods, the central task does not lie in demonizing said deities, nor in pretending that they do not exist. The question is, from the outset, centered on the need to establish a translation. On the need to convert a power that sells itself as nature into a form that is controllable, contestable and attributable, without which the will of the strongest once again operates as normality by sheer capacity for imposition. The ethics of this study is not born of the desire to punish technology for being technology. It is born of the commitment to prevent a decision organized by architecture from being demoted to chance, the rules of the game or technical necessity.

That is why the image of Dante Alighieri's <1>Inferno</1> was of interest from the start. His work exposes the degradation of the human bond when intelligence ceases to be an instrument of understanding and comes to operate as a ruse, producing an appearance of legitimacy in order to violate trust. Frictions are neutralized as technique, opacity becomes an element of strategy and the consumer is pushed to negotiate with the virtual world created by the supplier itself to satisfy its own interests.

To point a way forward, however, does not mean seeking a heroic gesture of demolition, as if it were desirable to put out the sun to solve the problem of the shadow. To point a way forward means proposing criteria capable of taming the asymmetry without destroying the infrastructure.

Here, the image of the Egyptian deities Isis and Ra<1><2>818</2></1> is able to compose the decisive ethical perspective. In the myth, the Sun-God does not cease to be the sun because someone hates him, nor does he lose <3>p. 792</3> his centrality through a mere desire for confrontation. What happens is subtler and much more important. Ra reigns over all, but is not invulnerable. His vulnerability appears in a minimal detail, a remnant of himself, an almost negligible trace of his own body. At the same time, Isis does not wish to annihilate the sun. It is not in her interest to replace the order of the world with one centered on herself by mere whim. Her interest is to force the sun to recognize that it is not absolute. To share with her part of his power.

Isis produces the serpent from the substance of Ra himself and, with that, turns the excess of power into an instrument for manifesting its limit. The venom does not destroy the Sun as a principle of the world. In exchange for the cure, Isis demands only that Ra reveal to her the name he keeps for himself. The name that does not circulate, that is not confused with titles, images or apparent manifestations of his grandeur. It is here that the analogy takes concrete form. The true name, in the myth, is neither a verbal ornament nor an irrelevant mystical secret. It is a “magic word”, almost like a command password. It is the point at which power and vulnerability cease to be pure force and enter the field of intelligibility. Isis does not long to know his name in order to humiliate him. She demands his name in order to transmute his power, establishing the control that then allows her to offer the cure. Once named, power ceases to operate as pure natural presence and becomes invocable, delimitable and, therefore, obliged to answer for its acts.

What Consumer Law lacks in the face of the <1>Lex Plataformae</1> is not moral indignation, nor a rhetorical repertoire of denunciation. It lacks the vocabulary to render demonstrable the decisions that today pass for the mere functioning of the system. The language to reconstruct a pattern and not merely react to an episode. It lacks a method to separate legitimate alteration from abusive degradation, ordinary mutability from normalized extraction, management of the environment from an exploitative program inscribed in the architecture. That is why the category of the Immaterial Object of Consumption and the criteria of open auditability and functional value equivalence do not appear, in the end, as dogmatic props. The concepts operate as a civilized version of the snake of the myth. They are the minimal mechanism that obliges power and, consequently, whoever wields it, to assume its own responsibilities.

To name is not to poeticize. To name is to move power from a regime of self-evidence to a regime of contestability. As long as the platform can say that it merely functions, merely updates, merely executes, merely applies rules, the conflict will remain trapped in the idiom of the inevitable. When, however, the regime of supply is reconstructed, when it is shown that access, permanence, visibility, reputation, intelligibility and enjoyment are organized by <1>p. 793</1> design and <2>enforcement</2>, what before seemed like weather once again seems like a decision. And what once again seems like a decision can be controlled. The name, here, is not the academic title of the thing. It is the condition of its limitation.

It is in this sense that the proposed protection is organized as an ethics of containment, not as an ethics of demolition. The aim is not to extinguish platforms, nor to romanticize a world without technique, something intellectually limiting and institutionally useless. The aim is to protect the functional integrity of the object acquired and the symbolic integrity of the consumer, recognizing that, under continuous consumption, value is not only technical utility, but place, sign, belonging and the possibility of social participation mediated by private infrastructure. When private power administers permanence, reputation, access and meaning, it already operates as practical normativity. The least the constitutional order can demand is that this power be translated into controllable criteria.

Law is not asked to put out the sun. It is asked to oblige it to say its name. It is asked that the platform cease to inhabit the comfortable zone of nature and accept the more demanding place of institutional responsibility. It is asked that what today presents itself as technical normality may once again be seen as choice, as program and, when necessary, as abuse. Only then will it be possible to restore degraded enjoyments, contest opaque decisions and rebuild trust without accepting that power organized by architecture present itself as a mere inevitable backdrop. To name, in the end, is not to adorn the world with words. It is to make even the sun obey, so that civilization may take back for itself the power to decide on the limits of its power.

Under such a horizon, the central legal question of this research consisted in verifying to what extent the normative structure of the Consumer Protection Code offers adequate protection to consumers inserted in continuous digital ecosystems, in which the enjoyment of what was acquired depends on stable private governance, ordinary mutability and opaque decisions incorporated into the very architecture of the supply.

Although historically read in light of the centrality of corporeal goods and discrete performances, Brazilian consumer law has settled into a robust instrument capable of offering adequate protection to consumers inserted in continuous digital ecosystems, even those in which value is less technical and more functional, economic, social or symbolic. These goods are concentrated in an immaterial ontology that, by its nature, depends on architecture, private curation, ordinary mutability and opaque regimes of decision.

The guiding hypothesis, confirmed in the end, was that the difficulty did not lie in an absence of normative basis, but in the persistence of an ontologically impoverished reading <1>p. 794</1> of the CDC itself. The Brazilian legal order already contains enough openness to accommodate the protection of these goods, provided that Art. 3, §1, is reread with a dogmatic density compatible with the contemporary informational economy. What was lacking was not a new legislative microsystem for the digital, but a conceptual reconstruction capable of removing the immaterial good from the residual position in which it was kept and bringing it back to the center of the protective regime. It is at this point that the Immaterial Object of Consumption presents itself as a category apt to name, qualify and make attributable conflicts that today tend to appear as technical inevitability.

The IOC makes it possible to show that, in platform markets, the immaterial product is not exhausted in content, access or utility considered in the abstract. It is constituted as enjoyment that is functionally maintained, governed and reconfigurable, dependent on technical infrastructure, private rules of circulation, visibility criteria, sanction mechanisms and forms of permanence in the ecosystem. Thus, the axis of analysis shifts from a static ontology of the good to a functional ontology of enjoyment. Instead of asking only what the object is in the abstract, it is now possible to ask under what conditions it remains usable, intelligible, recognizable and substantially equivalent to what justified the acquisition and sustained the consumer's legitimate expectation.

The reconstruction requires recognizing that, in continuous digital ecosystems, the relevant asymmetry does not fall only on the quantity of information available or on an abstract technical difficulty of understanding. It falls on the private means of producing meaning, expectation, comparability, trust and evidence. It was in this context that semiotic vulnerability proved a more precise category than the broad and diffuse vocabulary of “digital vulnerability”. The consumer is not vulnerable only because he knows less about the technology. He is vulnerable because the platform governs the way the object appears, the way loss is perceived, the language by which frustration is explained and the very limits of what can be reconstructed as a legally cognizable conflict.

It is shown that the injury, in these environments, frequently ceases to take the form of an isolated event and comes to operate as a program. Hence the formulation of abusive teleology as a category of unlawful act of architecture. Its meaning does not lie in generically moralizing design, nor in turning all mutability into suspicion. Its meaning lies in identifying situations in which opacity, friction, manufactured urgency, selective reconfiguration, asymmetry of reversal and normalization of small losses cease to be episodic occurrences and come to compose a method of exploitation incorporated into the very regime of supply. When this occurs, technique can no longer be treated as a neutral background. It appears as legally attributable conduct.

<1>p. 795</1> So that this attribution does not dissolve into generic criticism of the digital, the central <2>standards</2> of control are then proposed: open auditability and functional value equivalence. Open auditability is conceived to overcome the false alternative between absolute opacity and total transparency. Its core lies in asserting that Law need not demand full disclosure of code, proprietary databases or internal systems in order to exercise legitimate control over the supply. What it needs, rather, is sufficient institutional intelligibility about what relevantly interferes with enjoyment, sanction, visibility, access, the distribution of opportunities and the reconstruction of the conflict. Corporate opacity, however economically understandable it may be, cannot function as an immunity clause against the legal verifiability of what affects the consumer.

Functional value equivalence, in turn, is formulated to prevent the ordinary mutability of digital ecosystems from becoming a safe conduct for the unilateral degradation of the acquired experience. The point here is not to freeze the environment or to demand absolute stability in technically dynamic realities. The point is to assert that the lawfulness of the alteration cannot be gauged only by the nominal subsistence of the object, by the formal maintenance of access or by the abstract persistence of some residual utility. What matters is the substantial preservation of the function that legitimized the acquisition and structured the consumer's expectation. An object may continue to exist and, even so, no longer be, in a legally relevant sense, what was acquired. It is precisely to name this type of loss that functional value equivalence becomes decisive.

These two <1>standards</1> play a central role in the proposed regime because they supply a criterion for what would otherwise oscillate between technical reverence and intuitive indignation. It is they that make it possible to distinguish legitimate alteration from abusive degradation, a compatible update from an opportunistic reconfiguration, tolerable obscurity from immunizing opacity. Without open auditability, the critique of opacity risks becoming rhetoric without a knowable object. Without functional value equivalence, the critique of mutability risks becoming naive nostalgia for an impossible stability. With both, the thesis offers a yardstick of controllability capable of bringing the conflict back to the terrain of demonstration, attribution and institutional response.

The research also showed that this reconstruction does not require a break with intellectual property, but rather its reinscription in a constitutionally oriented key. In platform ecosystems, copyright, trademarks, <1>software</1> and other forms of exclusivity do not operate only as titles of appropriation over immaterial creations. They also function as legal technologies for organizing access, the sign, the interface and the very experience of enjoyment. For this reason, they cannot be read as a safe conduct for opportunistic <2>p. 796</2> mutability, structural precarization of the experience or absolute blocking of institutional controllability. The social function of property and of intellectual property requires that the exercise of these private positions remain compatible with duties of loyalty, verifiable stability, sufficient transparency, restoration and limitation of abuse in continuous consumer relationships.

The consequence of this constitutional reinscription of intellectual property becomes even clearer when one observes cases of termination of activities, discontinuation of services, abandonment of product lines or definitive shutdown of servers. As central components of contemporary life migrate to private digital ecosystems, the formal precariousness of use licenses can no longer be read as automatic authorization for the complete sacrifice of immaterial objects of consumption already incorporated into the existential, economic, relational and symbolic trajectory of the consumer. Photographs, histories, libraries, contact networks, progressions, projected identities, reputational positions and long-term investments cannot be legally treated as residues without density merely because they are technically housed in someone else's infrastructure.

The social function of property and of intellectual property prevents private exclusivity from operating as a title sufficient to legitimize the unilateral erasure of entire digital worlds under the pretext of business freedom, economic convenience or strategic reorientation of the supplier. The right to exploit, terminate or reorganize an activity is not to be confused with a supposed right to annihilate, without duties of transition, preservation or transfer, the functional enjoyment already stabilized in the consumer's sphere.

In continuous consumer relationships, there is no intellectual property right that sustains, by itself, the complete extinction of the infrastructure with the consequent complete sacrifice of the IOCs. If the termination of the service is unavoidable, the constitutional order requires that it be reconciled, as far as technically and legally possible, with solutions of continuity, portability, functional restoration, assignment of the operation or other measures suitable to prevent private architecture from becoming a lawful instrument of patrimonial and existential devastation of the consumer.

The limit case, at this point, is not only the opportunistic platform that alters rules, degrades functionalities or intensifies value extraction while it remains operating. It is also the platform that fails. When the functional value equivalence, the biographical continuity, the patrimonial memory and the accumulated sociability of thousands or millions of consumers depend on the permanence of servers, accounts, libraries, databases, authentication systems and execution environments, the technical or economic failure of the <1>p. 797</1> supplier may produce an even more radical form of loss. It is not only a matter of abusive alteration of the digital world, but of its possible erasure as an infrastructure of enjoyment. The question that emerges from this is whether Law will be able to keep treating business termination as a simple exercise of economic freedom when it results in the burial of collections, identities, reputations, histories and immaterial objects of consumption incorporated into consumers' practical lives.

It is on the remedial plane, however, that the proposed reconstruction reveals one of its most important consequences. If the injured bond is one of governed enjoyment, the legal response cannot be automatically reduced to the pricing of the harm. In IOC ecosystems, many injuries are not exhausted in the loss of a simple economic equivalent, because they fall on access, permanence, history, reputation, relational position, intelligibility of the experience and functional continuity of what was acquired. Treating every injury of this type as susceptible of merely pecuniary compensation means, in many cases, accepting that the supplier may unilaterally degrade, suppress or reconfigure enjoyment and then merely internalize the monetary cost of that conduct as an ordinary price of doing business. This is not adequate protection. It is automatic monetization of abuse.

For this reason, it is argued that the regime of remedies applicable to IOCs must be reorganized on the basis of a clear methodological priority. Whenever technically and legally possible, protection must aim at enjoyment, and not only at its later monetary translation. This means favoring functional restoration, reestablishment of access, reversal of relevant degradations, regime correction, cessation of opaque or exploitative practices and the imposition of minimum standards of verifiability on alterations that substantially affect the object acquired. Pecuniary compensation remains necessary in many cases, but it cannot occupy, by automatism, the position of sovereign remedy. When the injury is architectural, the response cannot be limited to pricing its effects; it must reach, as far as possible, the architecture that produced them.

This consequence is particularly important because it prevents Consumer Law from becoming a mere elegant administrator of normalized private losses. In platform markets, the automatic conversion of the conflict into money frequently keeps intact the structure that generated it. The consumer receives, at most, a late and imperfect equivalent, while the regime of supply keeps operating in the same way, ready to reproduce the same degradation at scale. By insisting on functional restoration and regime correction, the thesis seeks to put protection back in its proper place: not as a simple <1>p. 798</1> later compensatory calculation, but as a mechanism of institutional containment of recurring forms of exploitation inscribed in the very architecture of the experience.

The illustrative references mobilized throughout the thesis were not used as exhaustive sociological proof, nor as the basis for large-scale empirical generalizations, but as sufficient anchoring to bring out recurring mechanisms of governance by architecture, structural opacity, administration of trust, ordinary mutability and private production of the conditions of perception of the conflict. The usefulness of this material lay in showing that, in connected interactive entertainment environments, the value consumed may reside not only in a virtual item taken in isolation, but in access, progression, visibility, belonging, time, continuity of trajectory and symbolic position in the ecosystem.

There is, however, an additional consequence of this model which, although it was not explored over the course of the work with the centrality its gravity would deserve, imposes itself at least as an inescapable theoretical disquiet at the end of the journey. In continuous digital ecosystems, above all in sectoral models analogous to the one studied, the platform not only governs the enjoyment of the object acquired, but may progressively learn to decipher the very subject who enjoys it. What makes the problem singular is not a mere quantitative accumulation of data, but the qualitative density of the inferences that become possible when the user's experience is entirely mediated by proprietary infrastructure, by constant tracking systems and by interaction regimes designed to convert conduct into economic intelligibility.

In environments composed of dozens or hundreds<1><2>819</2></1> of diverse types and styles of risk and aggressiveness, of repeated patterns of choice, of progression routines, of responses to frustration and reward, of microdecisions made under pressure, of click cadences, of hesitations, insistences, deviations and recurrences, what is formed is not merely a database of declared preferences or registration identifiers. What is progressively formed is a private archive of dispositions, tendencies, propensities and behavioral structures whose depth comfortably exceeds the classical grammar of personal data traditionally addressed in the legal debate.

The point deserves special care because, in this scenario, the platform ceases to know the consumer only as an account holder, purchaser of content or recipient of <1>p. 799</1> targeted advertising. It comes to know him as a pattern. As predictability. As susceptibility. As a probable architecture of response to specific stimuli, calibrated frictions, intermittent rewards, visibility regimes and designs of scarcity. The asymmetry, then, is no longer limited to the informational plane in the current sense, nor is it exhausted in the supplier's technical superiority as to the internal functioning of the system. It shifts to a more delicate plane, in which the supplier comes to hold means of psycho-functional reconstruction of the user that the user himself does not possess about himself with an equivalent degree of operative precision. In structural terms, the platform not only sells, administers, reconfigures, rewards and sanctions. It may also observe, model, test, learn and feed back into the experience on the basis of a progressively refined knowledge of how that subject tends to act, insist, give in, become frustrated, persevere, consume and remain.

It is at this point that the hypothesis becomes even more disquieting. The relevant legal result of continuous digital consumption may consist not only in the formation of lasting bonds of functional, symbolic and economic dependence, but also in the repeated extraction of traces dense enough to map, with growing accuracy, psychological and dispositional profiles of high strategic value. In such a context, the platform no longer appears only as a supplier of Immaterial Objects of Consumption, nor only as a private administrator of persistent digital worlds. It appears, potentially, as a business structure capable of converting attention, gesture, preference, repetition, performance, decision-making style and pattern of interaction into economic intelligence about the practical interiority of its users.

The gravity of the problem lies in the fact that this knowledge is not gathered at the margins of the consumed experience, but produced within it, as an effect of the very architecture that organizes enjoyment, distributes visibility, doses reward, imposes sanction and stabilizes permanence. Economic exploitation thus ceases to fall only on what the consumer buys or uses and comes to touch, in an increasingly sophisticated way, the manner in which he is constituted as a legible subject before the platform itself.

This concern reinforces the central conclusion reached so far. If the category of goods comprised under the Immaterial Object of Consumption required specific protection because enjoyment was subjected to structural opacity, ordinary mutability and continuous private governance, this requirement intensifies when one perceives that the same ecosystems function, at the same time, as permanent laboratories of behavioral deciphering.

Semiotic vulnerability, from this angle, reveals an even deeper reach than initially formulated. It is not only a matter of the consumer being exposed to <1>p. 800</1> private regimes of production of meaning, expectation, trust and intelligibility of the conflict. It is also a matter of recognizing that these same regimes can operate as devices for extracting psychic knowledge about the consumer himself, expanding on an unprecedented scale the disproportion between who is read and who reads, between who is interpreted and who interprets, between who supplies traces of himself and who converts them into strategic power. The challenge that announces itself to Consumer Law, therefore, is not only that of limiting abusive mutations of enjoyment, but that of facing, in future development, the possibility that continuous platform consumption becomes a private technique for producing intensive subjective legibility, with consequences still insufficiently addressed for autonomy, for practical freedom and for the very integrity of personality in digitally governed environments.

This point helps explain why the conflict, in these environments, so often escapes the traditional categories of adjudication. The justice system frequently intuits that losses relating to accounts, digital goods, usage history and position in the environment exceed the immediate patrimonial dimension, but lacks a dogmatic grammar stable enough to turn this perception into rigorous reasoning. Hence the oscillation between two equally unsatisfactory reductions. Either the conflict is demoted to a low-density contractual annoyance, or it is perceived as intuitively serious without anyone being able to say precisely, in controllable legal language, what exactly was injured and why. One of the most relevant gains of this thesis lies in reducing this translation cost, providing categories apt to bring these conflicts back inside the CDC without inflating the system or abandoning it in favor of theories external to positive law.

To this extent, the main contribution of the research lies not in simply updating Consumer Law to keep up with technology, but in restoring institutional controllability to situations in which private power presents itself as nature, although it operates, in truth, as organized decision. The regime proposes to articulate coherently the qualification of the immaterial product by the Immaterial Object of Consumption, the location of the relevant asymmetry by semiotic vulnerability, the reading of governed expectation by hypercuratorial anticipation, the identification of the unlawful act by abusive teleology, the control of alterations by open auditability and functional value equivalence, the containment of exclusivity by the social function of property and of intellectual property and the reorganization of remedies around functional restoration and regime correction. With this, the aim is not to offer a total theory of platforms, but to prevent conflicts structurally produced by them <1>p. 801</1> from continuing to be treated as the simple natural price of inhabiting private systems supposedly impregnable to legal language.

At the same time, the aim is not to offer a total theory of digital consumption, nor to map exhaustively the plurality of platform ecosystems that today organize work, cultural circulation, sociability, economic intermediation and everyday experience. The focus remains concentrated on the theoretical-dogmatic reconstruction of the regime applicable to continuous immaterial goods in consumer relationships, having as its privileged field of intelligibility the environment of connected interactive entertainment. Nor is the aim to replace broad empirical research with illustrative exemplification, or to exhaust the institutional operationalization of the proposed standards. Open auditability and functional value equivalence will require, in the future, evidentiary maturation, refinement of expert examination and the development of decision-making protocols more sensitive to the structural opacity of platform conflicts.

The challenge posed by digital platforms lies in recognizing that, at the center of the contemporary informational economy, there are immaterial objects of consumption whose protection requires taking seriously the governed experience of the consumer in its functional, semiotic and symbolic dimension. The regime of the Immaterial Object of Consumption, as formulated here, aims to be an internal, structural and constitutionally oriented reconstruction of the CDC, apt to bring back into the field of responsibility what today still hides under the indifferent appearance of the mere functioning of the system.

The images mobilized throughout the thesis help condense, in the end, its ethical core. On one side, the problem worsens when intelligence, architecture and language cease to serve understanding and come to operate as a ruse that stabilizes the violation of trust; on the other, the adequate legal response does not consist in destroying the infrastructure, but in stripping it of the pretension of becoming unreachable or absolute, obliging private power to let itself be named, proven and limited. In an institutional key, this is exactly what Consumer Law lacks in the face of the <1>Lex Plataformae</1>: not empty indignation, but vocabulary and criteria capable of converting naturalized force into contestable and accountable power.

Such is the ethical and dogmatic core proposed here. What presents itself as the simple functioning of the system can and must be reconstructed as choice, as program and, when necessary, as abuse. The consumer, in continuous digital ecosystems, cannot remain reduced to the condition of a tolerated guest in someone else's world, subjected to unilateral reconfigurations without a language of contestation.

<1>p. 802</1> The Brazilian constitutional order does not require the elimination of the private infrastructures that organize contemporary experience; it requires, rather, that the power inscribed in them let itself be seen, proven, limited and, when necessary, corrected. In the end, the granted, revocable and reconfigurable floor that served as the starting point can no longer pretend to be nature. Once named, it comes to belong also to the field of responsibility, evidence, contestation, restoration and limit. For Law, force ceases to suffice unto itself and begins, at last, to answer to the name it bears.

In the Egyptian myth, Ra is the solar God and sovereign of the world, bearer of a secret name that concentrates his deepest power. Isis, wishing to access this power, gathers the saliva left by Ra, mixes it with earth and molds a serpent, which then bites the god himself. Wounded by a venom that no other being can remove, Ra suffers intensely. Isis then offers to cure him, but demands, as a condition, that he reveal his true name, hidden from all. Ra first tries to defend himself with his titles and apparent manifestations, but this is not enough. Only when he transmits the secret name to Isis can she neutralize the venom. The meaning of the tale lies not in a destructive defeat of the god, but in the idea that power only becomes truly accessible and limitable when it ceases to operate as pure inviolable presence and lets itself be named at its core. It is this logic that matters to the perspective under discussion. It is not a matter of eliminating technology or its powers, but of translating it into a language capable of allowing control and responsibility. <1>↩</1>

Abstract

This thesis investigates the interactive entertainment industry, organized through platform ecosystems and continuously provided electronic games, as a techno-legal infrastructure with significant impact on everyday life. It identifies the emergence of a private ordering grounded in architecture, curation, sanction, and unilateral mutation, here termed Lex Plataformae, whose operation challenges the traditional framework of the Brazilian Consumer Law, still oriented by a material ontology centered on discrete products and services, one-time deliveries, and static standards of conformity. It argues that such a framework fails to adequately capture the risks of platform-governed continuous enjoyment, since, in these markets, the consumed good does not appear as a stable thing, but rather as a functional and semiotic arrangement continuously modulated by the supplier. The thesis proposes the category of the Immaterial Object of Consumption (IOC) as an infrastructural concept capable of giving concrete form, within platform environments, to the notion of immaterial product set forth in Article 3, paragraph 1, of the Brazilian Consumer Protection Code as a governed enjoyment bundle. From this formulation onward, legal protection no longer focuses solely on the formal regularity of performance, but comes to encompass the functional integrity of the acquired object and the personal and symbolic integrity of the consumer. Within this framework, factual vulnerability is also reinterpreted in its semiotic dimension, insofar as the asymmetry involves a structural deficit in the consumer’s capacity to understand, anticipate, and control the regimes of signs, interfaces, functional promises, and symbolic rewards that compose the value of the IOC. On this basis, the thesis formulates the doctrine of the unlawful act of abusive teleology, under which abusiveness may arise not only from episodic failures, but from the very purpose inscribed in the architecture of the business model when designed to exploit the consumer’s semiotic vulnerability. In addition, it defends open auditability and functional value equivalence as criteria for legitimacy, controllability, and redress regarding unilateral mutations imposed over time. It further argues that the problem exceeds a strictly contractual and consumer-law grammar and reaches the constitutional level, insofar as it involves infrastructural private powers capable of affecting legally relevant consumer positions within environments of social participation governed by corporate actors. Methodologically, the research combines theoretical-constitutional reconstruction, consumer-law dogmatics, and a functional reinterpretation of intellectual property, in dialogue with critical theory of technology, platform sociology, political economy, anthropology of consumption, and semiotics. The Riot Games: League of Legends ecosystem is used as a locus of referenced exemplification through documentary analysis and situated observation of the functioning of the service and its ecosystem, without any claim to exhaustive empirical demonstration. In conclusion, the thesis argues that interactive entertainment IOCs must be recognized as legally protectable objects in contexts of continuous enjoyment and as loci of social participation under private infrastructure, thus becoming subject to a protective regime oriented by the object’s functional integrity, the consumer’s symbolic integrity, constitutional consumer protection, and the social function of intellectual property.

The sixth section carries out the dogmatic reconstruction, proposing an integrated reading of the 1988 Federal Constitution of the Federative Republic of Brazil, the Consumer Protection Code, and the Brazilian legislation on intellectual property rights based on the IOC regime, so as to make explicit criteria of legal qualification, correlative duties and possible institutional responses to conflicts on digital consumption platforms.<1>p. 42</1>

The seventh section concentrates illustrative applications and tests of fit of the proposed keys in typical contemporary situations of continuous digital consumption, using examples and public documentary material to make visible recurring patterns of friction, evidentiary requirements and blind spots in the translation of the conflict, without shifting the work toward an extended case study.<1>p. 42</1>
